doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 5, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Playing on chord changes: I Got Rhythm and song royalties
summary: Gibbs describes what goes through his head in fast solos, plays the song not the instrument, and explains how boppers wrote new tunes on old changes without being sued.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I was watching you recently on a video that went back to I think it was the Regis Philbin days, and it was a very uptempo thing, and you were wailing. And I was trying to imagine what is going through your head when you’re playing eighths and sixteenths at an uptempo song and the chords are moving quickly. Can you describe what’s happening in your head?

I’ll tell you the nearest way I can describe it is I don’t know who I’m talking to and I don’t know what I’m going to say. That’s how it is with playing. I haven’t got the slightest idea what you’re going to play but that’s coming out like I’m talking right now. I’m talking to you on a subject, I’m playing on chord changes and the song. I hear the song in my head. For example, I always tell everybody that, or young kids that want to play for me and show me how good they are or want to study: Don’t play the instrument, play the song. Like for example the chord changes to the song “I Got Rhythm” and the blues probably have more songs written on them than any other jazz piece in the world. If George Gershwin were alive and he could sue you for stealing chord changes, I would be in jail just like Dizzy Gillespie would be in jail. I’d have a good roommate, I’d have a good cellmate, but my point is that I’ve written about 30-40 songs, you know, if anybody knows these songs [scats] or [scats]. They’re “I Got Rhythm” chord changes. So when you’re playing “Ow” you don’t think of “I Got Rhythm” chord changes [scats]. That’s what I’m playing on. Not [scats] I’m not playing on “I Got Rhythm” I’m playing on “Ow” even though it’s the same chord changes. And you know that was one of the © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

secrets I found out about writing in the bebop era. They used to take all the great songs and, like “How High the Moon” and “Groovin’ High” and take the chord changes and write their own songs in them. Why should we be giving them all the money, you know? You know what’s wild, if you want to think back going way back, that Coleman Hawkins’ record of “Body and Soul” probably was one of the biggest records ever sold. He didn’t get five cents in royalty for writing it, and James Moody, who wrote “Moody’s Mood for Love” got sued for a while but he won because they called it “Moody’s Mood for Love” and he just used the chord changes. You can’t sue anybody for taking chord changes.
But you can sue them for stealing your melody you know?
